content:
We had a discussion some time ago about Turing machines being usable for sub-linear space and that this requires a read-only input tape and a write-only output tape. I have been thinking about a different way to define this that should be much better composable with different ways to define machines.

Let's assume we have a machine/computation model and a way for it to state that a certain machine m computes a function f in time t and space s. This machine model does not have to be able to compute in sub-linear space and it does not even have to be a Turing machine.

Now we take that machine model and use it instead of the "finite control" of a Turing machine:
A single step of the "outer" Turing machine consists of running the "inner" (potentially non-Turing) machine on the input symbol under the head plus some state data that we thread through. Once the inner machine terminates, we expect it to output a 4-tuple consisting of: (1) a potential symbol to write to the output, (2) an input head movement, (3) state to pass on to the next iteration and (4) a flag indicating termination.

We loop this step, threading through the provided state (but don't keep any other state of the inner machine between iterations) and keeping track of the input head position (bounding it at the input size, see previous discussions about log-log-space) until the inner machine flags termination.
The time requirement of the outer machine is the sum of the time spent in the inner machine and the space requirement is the max of the space used in the inner machine. Of course for complexity classes, the time and space requirements are then related only to the size of the original input, not the inputs to the inner machine.

If the state that is threaded through is small enough (assuming e.g. it's the full memory content), this model can easily represent logspace and even log-log-space computations, even if taken for itself alone, the inner model is not able to represent sub-linear space (looking at lambda calculus for example).

The nice thing about this way to define it is that we can use a very expressive language to model the inner machine and yet stay in the tight constraints imposed by the sub-linear space machine model.
This means it allows us to e.g. search inside a graph structure given as input and we don't have to describe this in a tedious way using explicit Turing machines.

Another big benefit is that we can model various other aspects of Turing machines using this model:

  1. Nondeterminism: For every iteration, we feed the inner machine a single nondeterministic bit,
    the outer machine accepts if there is some nondeterministic string such that it outputs "1". There have been proposals to model NP in cslib via polynomially-bounded witness languages. While this works for nondeterministic polynomial time, I think it fails to work for nondeterministic space (for example an NL machine can read polynomially many nondeterministic bits, but it cannot store them, so it is important that it cannot "re-read" nondeterministic bits it has already seen, which cannot easily be forbidden if they are just part of the regular input).

  2. Alternation: This works in the same way as nondeterminism and allows us to express and prove theorems like AP = PSPACE. Here, it is also important that "alternation bits" are to read again.

  3. Randomization: Same thing

  4. Oracles: We can model oracle tapes by allowing the inner machine to write symbol-by-symbol to a virtual oracle tape. We also allow it to output a "query the oracle" flag. Once this flag is set, the oracle answer is passed in with the next iteration, either symbol by symbol or as a full answer.

I have not really researched yet if this is a model that has been used elsewhere, but I think it is very close to how complexity theorists intuitively use these tools. Of course it might also be that this is all wrong and that it doesn't work that way :)
